newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia Hindus join annual body-piercing ritual.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia Hindus join annual body-piercing ritual.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of Malaysian Hindus on Thursday joined an annual procession to a holy cave, many of them piercing their bodies with hooks and skewers.
The festival, known as Thaipusam, is celebrated by Indians throughout the country, but nowhere is it as grand as in Batu (Stone) Caves, a limestone outcrop just outside the capital of Kuala Lumpur.
Thaipusam, a centuries-old Hindu tradition amongst Hindus of Southern Indian origin, is an annual affair in Malaysia and celebrated with far more fervour here than in India.

Devotees observe a rigorous regimen of spirituality in the month-long run up to the festival, including a dawn-to-dusk fast and a vegetarian diet. They must also abstain from alcohol, smoking and sex.
The day began for thousands with a dip in the river, although nowadays the authorities encourage devotees to use fresh water provided in large tanks instead, due to pollution.
After a session of prayers, many devotees went into a trance.

They then carried "Kavadis" -- elaborate frames mounted on their heads and shoulders and usually containing a Hindu deity -- up the 272 steps to a temple inside the cave, tossing their burden on to a heap before the Lord Murugan, the god of this celebration.
Tourists and devotees alike respectfully stepped out of the way of a continuous stream of kavadi carriers.

Some walked past with glazed eyes in deep trance; others, their tongues darting in and out and eyes flashing, screeched unnervingly, a manifestation of the Hindu spirits that are said to have taken over their bodies.

Although gaily decorated Kavadis, some standing several metres high, have become synonymous with Thaipusam, temple officials said they were reminding devotees that traditionally a jar of milk and a simple wooden structure carried on one shoulder would suffice.
